title: Letting Others Think They Are Right Says a Lot About Your Emotional Intelligence
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece argues that emotionally intelligent leaders know when to let go of being right in favor of preserving a relationship. It contrasts leaders who insist on correctness even over trivial matters with those who conserve their advocacy for issues that truly matter, arguing the latter group builds more trust and cooperation. The author is careful to note the limits of this approach: when a misconception could lead to a bad decision or safety risk, correcting the record still matters. Overall the article positions this as a subtle but telling marker of relational maturity in leadership.
points: Letting others believe they are right prioritizes the relationship over being technically correct
Leaders who insist on correctness even on minor issues tend to create resistance and disengagement
Smart leaders reserve their strong advocacy for genuinely meaningful topics
The exception: never let an inaccuracy stand if it could lead to a poor decision or safety risk
quotes: Letting others think they are right is a wise move in many situations. Especially when being “right” is less important or totally unimportant.
Allowing others to believe they are right privileges the relationship over accuracy and illustrates that the leader cares as much about harmony as they do about correctness.
Smart leaders conserve their strong advocacy for more meaningful topics and issues.
In fact, when personal safety is at stake, letting others believe they are right can be dangerous.
Good leaders prefer harmony over truth when the consequences are insignificant.
